extracted.intended_audience: BBC editors, programme makers, journalists and producers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and programme makers on when and how to grant anonymity to contributors and sources in BBC content, including technical, legal and editorial safeguards. Covers deciding when anonymity is justified, methods of disguising identity, recordkeeping, and risks such as jigsaw identification and court-ordered disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for offering anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity should be offered only when there is an editorial, legal, welfare or other justification for doing so. The programme maker must consider why the person wishes to remain anonymous. Do they have something to hide beyond their identity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The strongest rationale for granting anonymity is to protect the contributor from illegitimate retaliation, harassment or undesirable consequences for providing information. When it is not self-evident to the audience we should explain to them the reasons why the production granted anonymity to a source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to honour anonymity promises
rubrics_metrics.description: When we promise anonymity, we should make sure that we are in a position to honour that promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give careful consideration before offering a blanket guarantee of anonymity because disguising someone’s identity completely is difficult to achieve. Ensure the organisation can meet the promise in light of legal processes and operational records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify whom anonymity is from
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whom do you want to be anonymous from - from the general public or from people who know you well?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question determines the level of disguise required; disguising must take into account people who know the contributor well and distinctive features such as hair, gait and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping of anonymity agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: We should keep accurate and contemporaneous notes of conversations with sources and contributors about anonymity. A recording is preferable if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear evidence of what was promised and agreed to regarding anonymity to reduce misunderstandings and to help evaluate risks if disclosure is later sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of court orders and internal disclosure risks
rubrics_metrics.description: We must ensure when promising anonymity we take into account the implications of any possible court order demanding the disclosure of our un-transmitted or un-published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that materials that name them might have to be disclosed and could compromise anonymity (including notebooks, administrative paperwork, computer files, emails, video and audio rushes). Before taking action, a court order should be referred to Litigation to discuss which materials might compromise the anonymity of a contributor or source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate disguising for non-consensual/secret filming
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity may be necessary when we are unable to gain consent to show someone identifiably (e.g. when secretly filming for consumer or social research); the effort to disguise their identity should be proportionate to the private information that we might inadvertently reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people filmed are simply illustrative or not sufficiently culpable, disguise efforts should be balanced against the editorial need and the level of private information at risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal rights to anonymity and written waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people have legal rights to anonymity, including victims of some offences, including rape and others with a sexual element. Individuals can waive their anonymity, but they must do this in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure awareness of statutory anonymity protections and obtain written waivers where contributors elect to give them up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer blurring over pixelation; revoice over technical distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: When anonymity is essential, pictures should be blurred rather than pixelated, and contributions revoiced, rather than technically distorted, as both pixelation and technical distortion can be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blurring is preferable to pixelation because pixelation can be reversed. Revoicing (recording a voice-over by another person) is usually more effective than technically induced distortion or manipulation of voice pitch; audiences should be told if the voice is not that of the contributor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distinctive identifiers in images and audio
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that what may appear as insignificant detail (e.g. a piece of jewellery or the way a person walks) may reveal identity to those familiar with the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for tattoos, unusual watches, distinctive clothing, particular gestures, gait, or location. Be cautious using footage of someone walking filmed from behind since gait can be distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jigsaw identification prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken not to reveal several pieces of information in words or images that could compromise a person’s anonymity when put together: so-called 'jigsaw identification'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may require blurring house numbers, editing out certain pieces of information (spoken or otherwise), not revealing precise locations, and scrutinising other media to ensure combined reports do not reveal identity. Coordinate across outlets (e.g. web and broadcast) to avoid completing the jigsaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to the audience about anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is not self-evident to the audience we should explain to them the reasons why the production granted anonymity to a source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain reasons so audiences can judge a source's credibility and reliability; balance transparency with the need to protect contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider global and perpetual reproduction risks
rubrics_metrics.description: We should remember that whilst the story may be intended for particular BBC outlets, the story may well be transmitted or reproduced globally on other outlets without our knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider the safety of contributors whose identity may be inadvertently revealed internationally, in all media, in perpetuity; this affects decisions about how strongly to disguise identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain disguise methods and degree of protection to contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: When we grant anonymity it is important that the contributor is given sufficient information to be able to understand in advance what steps we propose to take, including the degree of protection that will result from any steps taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contributors understand exactly how their voice and/or image will be disguised (e.g. by using an actor’s voice, by blurring, pixelation or silhouetting). Judge the sensitivity of circumstances to set an appropriate level of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume contributor understands identifiability distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: It should not be assumed that a contributor will necessarily appreciate the fine distinction between not identifying them in BBC content and making sure they are not identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the difference and explain residual risks so contributors can make informed decisions about accepting anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial trade-offs when disguising identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting anonymity is not ideal for programme makers or for our audiences. Methods by which we disguise identities can sometimes compromise the content we publish visually and/or aurally through blurring the image or distorting the sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh loss of emotional impact or clarity against the level of anonymity promised; consider alternative storytelling approaches where disguising would unduly weaken the piece.
